name: Colin Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play trumpet in a theatre pit, the band area below the stage, teach brass at the town music school and do wedding jobs on Saturdays. I studied music at university. I'm a solid player after twenty years, though a cold morning still makes the first high note work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work fit around home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leena works at a pharmacy; we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The better theatre and wedding rates have given us nine months of expenses saved, and several schools and bands hire locally. I use a paper diary and the phone; I've never used an AI tool.

say: I'd welcome **quicker ticket emails** if they bring an audience to the theatre.
I'd remind the band that **live playing** still depends on people turning up.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and Leena's wage can absorb a delayed wedding balance.
I have **never used AI** and see no need to change my rehearsal diary for a plateau.
do: Confirm **signed spring calls** and renew six paid pupils for next term.
Save **eighty** from a cleared wedding balance after van fuel and children's bus passes.
feel: I feel **calm** because paid hours and savings cover a short billing delay.
S0.quote: I do not need a new tool to know when the theatre's rehearsal door opens.
fieldNote: His **higher rates** and nine months saved keep a delayed wedding balance from threatening the mortgage.
He keeps a **paper diary** and has never adopted AI, even for routine reminders.

steps.text: Confirm signed spring pit calls and renew six paid brass pupils
Save eighty from cleared wedding balance after fuel and bus passes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pit band that quicker ticket emails are fine if they help put people in seats. The horn still needs a player who turns up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little office software will not change my paid rehearsals or Saturday bookings much. Nine months saved and Leena's steady wage make a late wedding balance annoying rather than dangerous, though a mortgage always keeps me reading the dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll check the signed spring pit schedule with the stage manager and renew the six paid brass pupils for next term. After the next wedding balance clears, I'll put eighty into our house reserve once van fuel and the children's bus passes are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this version. A late fee can wait a few weeks when the teaching hours and savings are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a late wedding payment hurt the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One couple paid the last wedding instalment a month late. Leena and I used the normal account for groceries and left the reserve where it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use automatic rehearsal reminders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre offered an automatic rehearsal reminder last year, but I kept the paper diary. I copy the signed call times into it myself; I do not need a new tool to know when the theatre's rehearsal door opens.

say: I'd ask which **paid preparation hours** the theatre plans to remove.
I'd bring **contract figures** to the musicians association before accepting lower rates.
think: About **one-third of my pay** from arranging and booking could shrink.
Nine months saved cannot replace **recurring lost fees** while the mortgage stays monthly.
do: Compare **last season's invoices** with new theatre hours and bring the figures to the association this month.
Offer **extra school lessons** only with signed teaching fee, written room cost and five paying families.
Keep **pit dates** while the new class proves demand; refund deposits if the room falls through.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid preparation despite nearby teaching places.
S1.quote: Nine months saved would soften a cut but not pay a third of our mortgage forever.
fieldNote: He sees **arranging and booking fees** as a substantial part of his own income at risk.
His **extra class** needs signed pay, room terms and five paid families; he still declines untested AI charts.

steps.text: Bring last season's invoices and new theatre hours to musicians association
Offer extra school lessons only with written room cost, signed rate and five paying families
Keep pit dates; refund deposits if school room falls through

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre manager which paid arrangement and booking hours the new system removes. If fees change, I will take the contract to our musicians association with the other pit players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly a third of my income comes from copying parts, arranging wedding sets and booking players. Software may take those fees first, while I still have to practise and travel. Nine months saved would soften a cut but not pay a third of our mortgage forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll put last season's arranging invoices beside the theatre's new schedule and take the difference to the association. In the first year of change, I'll ask for more paid brass lessons at the school only if it offers a signed teaching rate and a room, and at least five families pay for a term. I'll keep my pit dates while we see if the extra class holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a real slice of pay. The local schools give me places to ask, but none has handed me five new pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that Tuesday school room actually yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school has an empty room on Tuesdays, but the principal has not offered it to me. I would get room cost and my teaching fee in writing before taking deposits, then refund families if the room falls through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let software make lesson charts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't let an automatic chart go straight onto a pupil's stand. Another teacher may use one, but I would want a live demonstration and check every note myself before even considering it.

say: I'd seek **written live dates** before AGI removes paid chart work.
I'd tell players **robots follow** full thinking AI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could erase preparation fees before robot players reach stages around 2031.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys a job search, not a permanent replacement wage.
do: List **four income streams** and request the next written theatre contract now.
Apply **after 2028** if preparation fees halve, but only for a posted, qualifying coach role with pickup and replacement written net pay.
Keep **pit and pupils** until a new contract; ask lender about full added interest before arrears if paid nights fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a large fee cut, with savings and local schools giving some control.
S2.quote: An advert is not my name on a payroll.
fieldNote: His **2028 screen-fee risk** arrives before robot trumpet playing around 2031.
He requires a **real vacancy**, qualifying bachelor's, feasible pickup and written net pay after travel before moving jobs.

steps.text: List pit, wedding, teaching and arranging pay; request written theatre contract
Apply after 2028 if fees halve and posted coach job accepts degree
Require pickup and written net pay after travel before leaving pit or pupils
Ask lender before arrears if nights fall; compare total added interest before signing relief

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre band that full AGI by 2028 can make charts and book players, but robots able to play trumpet follow around 2031. I want paid live dates in writing before the screen fees disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Copying, arranging and booking could be cheaper to buy from AGI almost at once. I may still have a chair in the pit, yet losing those extra fees would take a large piece of our income; Leena's pay and nine months saved give us a search, not another lifetime wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list the last year's pit, wedding, lesson and arranging pay and ask for the next theatre contract in writing. In the first year after 2028, if preparation income halves, I'll apply for a posted brass-coach role at another local school only if my bachelor's meets its rules, school pickup works and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I will keep the pit and existing pupils until another contract is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, because a third of the money could go while the mortgage stays put. There are schools nearby. An advert is not my name on a payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there an open brass-coach job today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school listed a brass job in August and filled it. I can ask about the next opening without telling Leena that we've already got it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pit cuts nights too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pit also cuts paid nights, I'll ask our lender about a short payment change before arrears. Leena and I would add up all the extra interest before we sign anything.

say: I'd ask for **signed player rates** and deposits on wedding jobs.
I'd price a **live brass workshop** before inviting anyone to pay.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens charts and booking before robot horns arrive around 2034.
**Preparation fees** could thin sooner, though paid live bookings may last.
do: Put **written player rates** and deposit deadlines on new wedding quotes this season.
Offer **workshop** if preparation fees fall, with written hire/insurance, safe storage, separate mouthpieces and six prepayments covering costs and teaching.
Repeat **after 2031** only if six paid places and hall terms hold; refund if bookings stop at four.
feel: I feel **anxious** about earlier fee loss but can test a paid live class without using savings.
S3.quote: Six paid brass-workshop places are the floor for room hire and my teaching hours.
fieldNote: His **workshop gate** protects paid teaching time and the household reserve from uncertain hall demand.
He requires **written insurance and storage** and separate mouthpieces before running a safe brass session.

steps.text: Quote written wedding player rates and deposit deadlines
Book workshop if preparation fees fall, with written hire/insurance/storage, six paid places and separate mouthpieces
Require six prepayments to cover teaching time; refund four buyers if short
Repeat after 2031 only while six places and hall conditions hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the wedding band we have five years to keep live work properly priced, not give away every rehearsal. I would ask clients for a signed player rate and a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could write the arrangements and handle booking, and robots able to play horns may follow around 2034. Ordinary tools might trim those preparation fees sooner; live weddings could hold, but only if the bookings and payments are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I'll put a written player rate and deposit deadline on new wedding quotes, and I'll keep the theatre dates already signed. By 2031, if preparation fees fall, I'll offer a separate Saturday brass workshop at the community hall only if its hire and insurance are written, six adults prepay enough to cover them and my teaching time, and the hall approves safe instrument storage. In the first year after AGI, I'll repeat it only if those paid places and conditions hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about screen fees falling while we still need the mortgage payment. I would like another live income stream, but I will not spend our reserve to fill empty chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the hall booked, and what if only four pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall manager has mentioned Saturdays, not offered a signed room. If only four adults pay, I would refund them and wait. Six paid brass-workshop places are the floor for room hire and my teaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the workshop handle shared instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring my own cleaned mouthpieces for demonstrations and ask people to bring their own horns. Nobody shares a mouthpiece, and I will not advertise the workshop until the hall confirms storage and insurance.

I'd tell the theatre a **ten-year plan** needs signed rates.

**Chart fees** may fall before 2036, while robot players follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger pit players that ten years is long enough to ask for proper pension contributions and fewer unpaid calls. I would take a written proposal to the musicians association, not rely on a promise from the theatre manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 and still have a mortgage, while robot players might enter venues around 2039. Chart fees may disappear earlier, but a decade lets us build the reserve and shift more hours into live teaching if the school will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the association to compare pension contributions and paid rehearsal calls across local theatres. By 2036 I'll aim for twelve months of expenses saved from spare paid lessons and cleared wedding balances after household bills. In the first year after AGI, if the pit cuts paid hours, I'll apply for a posted full-time brass-teacher job only if my bachelor's qualifies, the school timetable lets us collect the children and a signed net offer after travel covers the mortgage; I'll keep current pupils until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because chart fees may fall before 2036, even with nine months saved. Ten years and nearby schools give me time. The mortgage makes a paper promise worth less than a signed rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the association promise pension changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association can bring the rehearsal sheets to the theatre, but I will not assume it can win a pension increase. I will keep the current paid calls while it negotiates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a full-time school job waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full-time school role is not open today. Leena and I would check any actual offer against pickup and the mortgage before I give notice at the music school.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the chart and booking fees could go before another school offers paid hours. Written pit dates, a real qualified vacancy and the lender's total costs if live nights also fall would let us choose calmly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays a musician for setting up and packing away. A paid call starts when the player arrives with the case, not at the first note.

headlineQuote: A paid call starts when the player arrives with the case, not at the first note.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old trumpet player** with a music bachelor's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
His **higher pay** and nine-month reserve buy time, though arranging and booking make a third of income.
He **never uses AI** and prefers signed calls, paper dates and live playing.
He would seek **paid teaching** and association terms before leaving current pupils for another school.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove chart and booking fees before replacement school hours appear.
whatWouldHelp: **Written pit dates**, a posted qualifying school role and full lender costs would help him decide.
